Why Brisbane generates ET demand

Brisbane serves the Queensland CSG-to-LNG chain — the three Curtis Island trains and their upstream gathering — alongside the Bowen Basin coal industry, its heavy-haul railways, and the state's power fleet.

LNG plant exchangers and the fin-fan fleet supporting liquefaction take eddy current examination between runs, where tube failure means capacity loss on a scheduled cargo.

Wire ropes on winders and draglines are examined electromagnetically, and processing-plant exchangers bring conventional eddy current into mining scope.

Condenser and feedwater heater tubing is eddy current's core power-generation work — full-bundle screening each major outage with plugging decisions made tube by tube.

Rolling-contact fatigue on the railhead is screened with eddy current from inspection vehicles, complementing the ultrasonic programme.

What typically gets examined

In practice that means ET work across LNG trains on Curtis Island, upstream compression and gathering, draglines and CHPP plant in the Bowen Basin, coal rail infrastructure, and power stations — with scope set by the damage mechanisms each asset actually runs, not by a standard menu.

Certification and acceptance in Brisbane

AS/NZS standards and AINDT certification are the baseline, with Queensland's coal mining safety legislation adding site competency requirements; LNG operators run integrated turnaround regimes where NDT slots are booked far ahead.

Examinations themselves are performed to ASME Section V Article 8 and its tubing appendices, ISO 15548, and ASTM E243 for tube examination. The evidence chain — technician certification current on the day, instrument and reference block calibration, and the procedure revision in force — travels with every report, because that bundle is what an audit actually checks.
